title: ભારતીય શાસ્ત્રીય નૃત્ય: ઉદ્ભવ, માન્ય સ્વરૂપો અને મૂળભૂત સંકલ્પનાઓ
body:
અર્થ અને ઐતિહાસિક વિકાસ

ભારતીય શાસ્ત્રીય નૃત્ય એવી પ્રદર્શિત કલા છે જેમાં લયબદ્ધ હલનચલન, સંગીત, અભિવ્યક્તિ, કથાકથન અને સ્થાપિત કલાત્મક પરંપરાઓનો સમન્વય થાય છે. દરેક શાસ્ત્રીય નૃત્ય પરંપરાનો પોતાનો કાર્યક્રમક્રમ, પ્રાદેશિક સંગીત પરંપરા, વેશભૂષા અને અર્થ વ્યક્ત કરવાની રીતો હોય છે.

Indian dance has a long cultural history. The bronze Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, dance figures in ancient sculptures and medieval temple carvings provide evidence of the importance of dance in Indian society. The dancing form of Shiva as Nataraja, which attained a particularly developed sculptural form during the Chola period, represents the close relationship between dance, religion and Indian art.

Such archaeological evidence establishes the antiquity of dance in India. However, it does not establish that every modern classical dance existed in its present form during the ancient period. The recognized classical dances developed through centuries of regional cultural exchange, religious patronage, artistic innovation and institutional preservation.

Traditional centres of development

  • Temples: Religious rituals and devotional performances supported traditions such as Bharatanatyam and Odissi.
  • Royal courts: Royal patronage contributed to the development of Kathak, Bharatanatyam and Mohiniyattam, among other forms.
  • Religious monasteries: The Vaishnava monasteries of Assam preserved Sattriya.
  • Modern cultural institutions: Academies, universities and training centres have helped preserve and popularize classical dance beyond its original regional settings.

The 8 recognized classical dance forms

The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training identifies 8 principal recognized classical dance forms of India. The following classification reflects its published position as consulted on 25 November 2026.

Classical danceTraditional region of origin
BharatanatyamTamil Nadu
KathakNorthern India
KathakaliKerala
MohiniyattamKerala
KuchipudiAndhra Pradesh
OdissiOdisha
ManipuriManipur
SattriyaAssam

Kathak is particularly associated with Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, although its historical development extends across northern India. Kerala is associated with 2 of the 8 principal classical forms.

The classification of an art form as classical does not imply that folk traditions are artistically inferior. Folk dances may also require considerable skill, have established conventions and convey religious or historical themes.

Foundational texts

TextTraditional authorImportance
Natya ShastraBharata MuniFoundational treatise on drama, dance, music and aesthetic expression
Abhinaya DarpanaNandikeshvaraImportant treatise on dance gestures and expression
Sangita RatnakaraSharngadeva13th-century treatise covering music and dance

The Natya Shastra provides a shared theoretical foundation for Indian classical performing arts. Individual dance traditions nevertheless draw upon different regional texts, literary compositions and systems of training.

Basic components of classical dance

Classical Indian dance distinguishes between rhythmic movement, expressive dancing and dramatic representation.

  • Nritta: Pure dance, emphasizing rhythm and patterns of movement without necessarily communicating a particular story.
  • Nritya: Expressive dance in which movement and gestures communicate emotions, meanings or literary compositions.
  • Natya: Dramatic representation involving characters, situations and narrative action.

These components may appear together in a single performance. For example, a dancer may present rhythmic movement, interpret the emotional meaning of a song and subsequently portray a character from an epic.

Abhinaya: communication through performance

Abhinaya refers to the means through which a performer communicates the meaning and emotional content of a performance to the audience.

Type of abhinayaPrincipal means of expression
AngikaBody movements, gestures and facial expressions
VachikaSpeech, dialogue and vocal expression
AharyaCostumes, ornaments, makeup and other external elements
SattvikaPhysical expression of internal emotional states

Bhava is the emotional state represented through performance, while rasa is the aesthetic experience produced in the audience.

The commonly taught Navarasa classification includes Shringara (love), Hasya (laughter), Karuna (compassion or sorrow), Raudra (anger), Vira (heroism), Bhayanaka (fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder) and Shanta (tranquillity). The earlier classical formulation of 8 rasas was subsequently expanded through the acceptance of Shanta.

Tandava and Lasya

Tandava is conventionally associated with vigorous expression and the dance of Shiva. Lasya emphasizes grace, gentleness and delicate expression and is traditionally associated with Parvati. These qualities are not restricted to performers of a particular gender.

Prelims focus

  • The principal recognized classification contains 8 classical dances.
  • Kathakali and Mohiniyattam both originate in Kerala.
  • Natya Shastra is attributed to Bharata Muni.
  • Abhinaya Darpana is attributed to Nandikeshvara.
  • Costume and makeup belong to Aharya Abhinaya.
  • Trap: Nritta emphasizes rhythmic movement; Nritya communicates meaning and emotion; Natya represents drama.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 9, pp. 126–127; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 7, pp. 107–108; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 12–14 (online edition used because the project copy was unreadable); CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 1–5; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, performing arts overview. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Bharatanatyam: Temple Traditions and the Tanjavur Repertoire
body:
Origin and historical development

Bharatanatyam originated in Tamil Nadu and developed particularly through the temple and court traditions of the Tanjavur region. Its historical predecessors were known by names such as Sadir and Dasi Attam.

Temple dancers associated with the Devadasi tradition and hereditary dance teachers known as Nattuvanars played important roles in preserving its repertoire. Its artistic development also benefited from patronage in the royal courts of southern India.

The sculptures of the Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram and the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur illustrate the historical connection between dance and temple art in Tamil Nadu.

The Tanjore Quartet

During the early 19th century, the 4 brothers collectively known as the Tanjore Quartet helped organize the Bharatanatyam repertoire into a structured recital.

  • Chinnayya
  • Ponnayya
  • Sivanandam
  • Vadivelu

They were associated with the Tanjavur court during the reign of the Maratha ruler Serfoji II. Their contribution lay primarily in organizing and developing an existing dance tradition rather than inventing Bharatanatyam.

The traditional repertoire

A structured Bharatanatyam recital is commonly known as the Margam. It gradually introduces the different dimensions of classical dance, beginning with introductory rhythmic movement, developing into expressive compositions and concluding with a lively presentation.

  1. Alarippu: An introductory rhythmic composition.
  2. Jatiswaram: Pure dance combining musical notes and rhythmic movement.
  3. Shabdam: A composition introducing expressive interpretation of words and stories.
  4. Varnam: A major composition combining rhythmic dance with elaborate expressive passages.
  5. Padam and Javali: Expressive compositions often dealing with devotion, love and human emotions.
  6. Tillana: A predominantly rhythmic composition usually presented near the conclusion of a recital.

An invocation may precede the main sequence, and a Mangalam, or auspicious conclusion, may follow it. Contemporary recitals do not necessarily include every item in the same order.

Music and visual characteristics

Bharatanatyam is accompanied by Carnatic music. Common instruments include the mridangam, violin, veena and flute. The Nattuvanar guides the rhythmic structure of the performance through vocal rhythmic syllables and small cymbals, a practice called Nattuvangam.

The costume commonly includes a specially arranged silk garment with a prominent pleated fan at the front. Temple-style jewellery, ankle bells and decorative hair ornaments are characteristic. The opening of the pleated fan during bent-knee positions makes the costume particularly recognizable.

Modern revival and major exponents

During the late colonial period, hereditary dance traditions faced social stigma and restrictions. In the 20th century, artists and reformers helped establish Bharatanatyam on the modern public stage.

ExponentContribution or association
Rukmini Devi ArundaleEstablished Kalakshetra in 1936 in present-day Chennai
E. Krishna IyerAdvocated the revival and public acceptance of Bharatanatyam
T. BalasaraswatiProminent exponent of expressive dance and hereditary performance traditions
Yamini KrishnamurthyRenowned exponent of Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi
Mrinalini SarabhaiPromoted classical dance through Darpana Academy in Ahmedabad

Kalakshetra became an important institution for systematic instruction in Bharatanatyam, Carnatic music and related arts. The tradition also continues through hereditary teachers, independent dance schools and university programmes.

Prelims focus

  • Traditional origin: Tamil Nadu, particularly Tanjavur.
  • Sadir and Dasi Attam are historical predecessors of Bharatanatyam.
  • The Tanjore Quartet organized the traditional repertoire in the 19th century.
  • Alarippu, Varnam and Tillana are important Margam items.
  • Music: Carnatic; principal percussion instrument: mridangam.
  • Rukmini Devi Arundale established Kalakshetra in 1936.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 12; CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 4–7; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Cultural Packages, Bharatanatyam Dance; Kalakshetra Foundation, institutional history; UPSC Education, Classical Dances of India — Eight Forms, Bharatanatyam section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Kathak: Storytelling, Court Patronage and Gharanas
body:
Origin in northern India

The name Kathak is derived from the word Katha, meaning story. Its historical roots lie in the storytelling traditions of northern India, where performers communicated religious narratives through music, gestures and expressive movement.

During the 15th and 16th centuries, the spread of the Bhakti movement contributed to the development of Kathak as a distinct dance tradition. Narratives about Radha and Krishna and performances associated with Rasa Lila became important sources of inspiration.

Development under royal patronage

Kathak subsequently flourished in the courts of Mughal rulers, regional nobles and Rajput rulers. Court patronage contributed to the development of its rhythmic complexity, presentation and costume traditions.

Wajid Ali Shah, the last Nawab of Awadh, was an important patron of Kathak in the 19th century. Lucknow became a particularly influential centre of the dance.

During British rule, Kathak faced social and official disapproval. Nevertheless, hereditary performers, including courtesans and professional teachers, helped preserve its traditions. Its subsequent development as a recognized classical dance reflects contributions from both devotional and courtly traditions.

Major gharanas

A gharana is a school or lineage of artistic training with distinctive stylistic conventions. The Kathak gharanas are not separate classical dances; they are traditions within Kathak.

GharanaPrincipal centreCharacteristic emphasis
LucknowAwadh, Uttar PradeshGrace and expressive interpretation
JaipurRajasthanRhythmic complexity and vigorous footwork
BanarasVaranasi, Uttar PradeshDistinctive rhythmic compositions and traditional presentation
RaigarhChhattisgarhCourt-supported development drawing upon different Kathak traditions

The Raigarh tradition benefited from the patronage of Raja Chakradhar Singh. The Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras gharanas are the best-established historical names commonly associated with Kathak, with Raigarh also recognized as an important later school.

Repertoire, music and costume

Kathak is recognizable through intricate rhythmic footwork, ankle bells and repeated graceful turns. Rhythmic footwork is known as Tatkar, and turns are commonly called Chakkars.

A performance may include an invocation, pure rhythmic compositions such as Tukra, Toda and Paran, and expressive items such as Gat Bhav or the interpretation of a Thumri. Thumri is a form of Hindustani vocal music especially suited to expressive interpretation.

Kathak primarily uses Hindustani classical music. Common accompanying instruments include the tabla, pakhawaj, sarangi and harmonium.

Costumes reflect its different historical traditions. Women may wear a lehenga and choli with a veil or a long flared Angarkha-style garment with churidar trousers. Men commonly wear a kurta with churidar or dhoti. Ghungroo, or ankle bells, help make the dancer's rhythmic footwork audible.

Major exponents and institutions

ExponentAssociation
Birju MaharajLucknow gharana
Shambhu MaharajLucknow gharana and expressive Kathak
Sitara DeviProminent Kathak exponent
Gopi KrishnaProminent Kathak dancer and choreographer
Kumudini LakhiaFounder of Kadamb Dance Centre, Ahmedabad

Kathak Kendra in New Delhi is a constituent institution of the Sangeet Natak Akademi dedicated to Kathak training and development.

In Gujarat, Kumudini Lakhia contributed particularly to the development of group choreography in Kathak. Her establishment of Kadamb in Ahmedabad made the city an important centre of classical dance education.

Prelims focus

  • Kathak derives its name from Katha, meaning story.
  • Its development reflects both Bhakti and royal court traditions.
  • Wajid Ali Shah was an important patron of the Lucknow tradition.
  • Music: Hindustani; characteristic instruments include tabla and pakhawaj.
  • Kumudini Lakhia is associated with Kathak and Kadamb, Ahmedabad.
  • Trap: Kathak is a northern Indian dance; Kathakali is a distinct dance-drama from Kerala.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 9, pp. 126–127; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 13; CBSE, Class 12, Dance: A Survey, Kathak section, pp. 8–10; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Kathak Kendra institutional history; Government of India, Padma Vibhushan citation for Kumudini Lakhia, 2025; UPSC Education, Classical Dances of India — Eight Forms, Kathak section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Kathak develops from northern religious storytelling through Bhakti and court patronage, survives through hereditary performers and courtesans, and reaches the modern stage.
pictures.caption: Development of Kathak from storytelling to the modern stage.
